title: 45-year-old man with severe headache and very high blood pressure
presenting_complaint: Severe headache and blurred vision for 4 hours, found to have blood pressure 220/130.

history_items.question: Ask about headache character
history_items.finding: Severe, throbbing, worst headache of his life, started suddenly.
history_items.evidence_basis: Severe sudden headache with markedly elevated BP raises concern for hypertensive emergency with end-organ threat.

history_items.question: Ask about visual symptoms
history_items.evidence_basis: Visual symptoms suggest possible hypertensive retinopathy/end-organ involvement.

history_items.question: Ask about antihypertensive compliance
history_items.finding: Stopped his amlodipine 3 weeks ago due to cost.

history_items.question: Ask about chest pain
history_items.evidence_basis: Screens for concurrent ACS/dissection, which would change management urgency/approach.

examination_items.evidence_basis: Papilledema confirms hypertensive emergency with end-organ damage, not just severe uncomplicated hypertension.

examination_items.finding: No focal deficits, alert and oriented.
examination_items.evidence_basis: Absence of focal deficit argues against acute stroke, though does not exclude it entirely.

examination_items.finding: Normal heart sounds, no signs of heart failure.

investigations.name: Urinalysis
investigations.evidence_basis: Renal involvement supports a diagnosis of hypertensive emergency rather than uncomplicated severe hypertension.

investigations.name: CT head (non-contrast)
investigations.result_detail: Excludes an acute intracranial bleed as the cause of the headache.
investigations.evidence_basis: Important to exclude hemorrhagic stroke, which would change management significantly.

investigations.name: Renal function (creatinine)
investigations.result_summary: Creatinine 168 µmol/L (elevated from a baseline of 90).
investigations.result_detail: Acute kidney injury, supporting end-organ damage.
investigations.evidence_basis: Acute renal impairment is a defining feature of hypertensive emergency.

differentials.name: Severe hypertension without acute end-organ damage

clinical_decisions.label: Admit for controlled IV antihypertensive titration with close monitoring, targeting a gradual BP reduction
clinical_decisions.rationale: Correct: confirmed end-organ damage (papilledema, AKI, proteinuria) makes this a hypertensive emergency requiring controlled, monitored IV therapy — not rapid oral dosing at home.

clinical_decisions.label: Give an oral antihypertensive dose and discharge home with a GP follow-up in a week
clinical_decisions.rationale: Unsafe: end-organ damage (papilledema, AKI) means this needs monitored inpatient BP control, not outpatient management.

outcome_branches.title: Appropriate controlled management
outcome_branches.narrative: BP is carefully lowered over 24-48 hours with IV labetalol, headache and vision improve, renal function recovers, and he is discharged on an optimized oral regimen with close follow-up.
outcome_branches.educational_explanation: Confirmed end-organ damage requires monitored, controlled BP reduction — too-rapid lowering risks organ hypoperfusion, but untreated/undertreated crisis risks ongoing damage; inpatient titration balances both.

outcome_branches.title: Unsafe discharge
outcome_branches.narrative: He returns two days later with worsening renal function and a further rise in creatinine, requiring admission and a more difficult recovery than if treated promptly.
outcome_branches.educational_explanation: Discharging a patient with confirmed end-organ damage (papilledema, AKI) without monitored inpatient management is unsafe — the presence of end-organ signs is what distinguishes an emergency from simple severe hypertension.

counterfactual_branches.alternative_action_label: What if you had skipped fundoscopy?
counterfactual_branches.alternative_evidence: Papilledema is one of the clearest bedside signs distinguishing hypertensive emergency from severe-but-uncomplicated hypertension.
counterfactual_branches.probability_effect: Substantially lower confidence in the emergency classification without it.
counterfactual_branches.potential_outcome: Risk of undertreating a true emergency as if it were uncomplicated severe hypertension.
counterfactual_branches.reasoning_lesson: A hypothesis-driven exam finding (fundoscopy here) can be as decisive as a lab test in distinguishing a true emergency from a look-alike.

reasoning_error_catalog.label: Poor investigation selection
reasoning_error_catalog.educational_note: Renal function is central to classifying this as an emergency vs. uncomplicated severe hypertension.

reasoning_error_catalog.label: Ignoring red flags
reasoning_error_catalog.trigger: e_fundoscopy not performed before the final decision.
reasoning_error_catalog.educational_note: Skipping the single exam finding most likely to confirm end-organ damage.

ml_feature_hint.note: See docs/DATASETS.md for the dataset's empirical (non-standard) cp/exang encoding used here.

references: Standard MBBS-level hypertensive emergency vs. uncomplicated severe hypertension teaching distinction (end-organ damage as the key discriminator).
